Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified an evolving fake-download campaign targeting users searching for cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, and unofficial utilities. The campaign uses trojanized Inno Setup-style installers to distribute multiple monetized software payloads, referred to by the delivery system as “offers”, during a single installation session.

Our investigation found that the installers use a per-offer callback and status-tracking model to manage delivery and record installation outcomes. We confirmed three downstream monetization branches that transformed affected devices into monetized assets, including by routing third-party internet traffic through the device, enrolling it in a distributed-computing platform, or installing additional utility-style software, often without users’ informed knowledge or consent. These products and components may have legitimate uses, but their silent installation through deceptive software bundles without informed user consent introduces security and privacy risks.

Organizations can reduce their exposure to this activity by preventing the use of untrusted software sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and monitoring for unexpected software installations and persistence mechanisms.

This blog details the campaign’s execution model and confirmed outcomes and provides mitigation guidance, Microsoft Defender protection information, advanced hunting queries, MITRE ATT&CK mappings, and indicators of compromise to help defenders identify, investigate, and respond to related activity.

Attack chain overview

The fake-download campaign follows a four-stage attack chain that progresses from deceptive lures through Inno-based staging, offer-controlled payload delivery, and installation of one or more monetization branches:

Initial access via fake download lures – Users run fake installers promoted as cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, executors, or unofficial utilities.

Inno wrapper execution and temporary runner staging – The installer launches an Inno Setup-style temporary runner under %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\, which starts recurring eld*.exe, set_*.exe, or other numbered stages.

Offer execution callback and payload delivery – The runner contacts rotating infrastructure using a repeatable d=inno and r=offer_execution callback pattern. Offer, affiliate, download-network, placement, and session values coordinate downstream payload selection and correlate activity within the installer session.

Final payload installation and monetization – Staged payloads use unattended installation switches to install one or more confirmed campaign branches: WorldProxyPool for proxy and network-resource monetization; CharityEngine and Berkeley Open Infrastructure for Network Computing (BOINC) for compute-resource monetization; or Advanced Windows (AW) Manager and Windows Manager for adware-style utility monetization. WorldProxyPool also creates recurring SYSTEM scheduled tasks for agent startup, watchdog execution, and updater activity.

Across the investigated activity, user-launched lures spawned Inno Setup-style temporary runners under %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\ and then launched one or more numbered eld*.exe stages. The depth of the execution chain and its downstream outcome varied by installer session. One Echo Client example progressed through multiple numbered stages and reached several monetization branches, while other observed lures exposed fewer numbered stages or downstream components.

Offer execution callback and payload delivery

After staging, the Inno temporary runner contacted rotating callback infrastructure using randomized URL paths but a repeatable query-string structure:

http:///?sis=&fz=&d=inno&r=offer_execution&ko=no&o=&a=&dn=&spot=&t=&cr=

Failed or blocked offers used r=offer_execution_fail and sometimes included local error text, including messages that the operation did not complete because the file contained a virus or potentially unwanted software. These callbacks are useful campaign-attribution and sequencing markers, but they are not always the earliest prevention point. In some endpoint detection and response (EDR) traces, child payloads launched before or around the r=offer_execution callback.

The campaign used offer IDs, affiliate IDs, download-network IDs, and placement values to select or report downstream payload attempts. Observed offer and download-network combinations included o=1712 / dn=507, o=1720 / dn=536, o=1727 / dn=564, o=1729 / dn=566, o=331 / dn=244, o=1674 / dn=440, o=1675 / dn=441, o=1681 / dn=447, and o=1730 / dn=567. Different offers could succeed or fail independently within the same installer session, so a failed first offer did not necessarily mean that the full bundle stopped.

Final payload installation and monetization

After offer callback and payload delivery, the campaign launched downstream installers or components using unattended installation switches such as /qn, /S, /quiet, and /norestart. This stage converted the fake-download execution chain into installed software and recurring execution across three monetization branches: proxy and network-resource monetization, compute-resource monetization, and adware-style utility monetization.

Proxy and network-resource monetization — WorldProxyPool

In the WorldProxyPool branch, a staged eld4.exe payload created three SYSTEM-level scheduled tasks for components under C:\Program Files\WorldProxyPool\. WorldProxyPoolAgent configured sdk-agent.exe to run at system startup with highest privileges; WorldProxyPoolWatchdog configured a hidden, noninteractive PowerShell watchdog script to run every five minutes; and WorldProxyPoolUpdater configured sdk-agent.updater.exe update to run hourly. The installer also started the agent task immediately with schtasks.exe /Run. Subsequent task launches were brokered by the Windows Task Scheduler service (svchost.exe -k netsvcs -p -s Schedule), causing sdk-agent.exe and the watchdog script to execute in the service context. This persistence mechanism supports recurring proxy-agent, watchdog, and updater activity, consistent with network-resource monetization.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft recommends the following actions to reduce exposure to this campaign and detect related activity:

Preventive controls

Avoid untrusted software sources. Do not download cracked software, key generators, unofficial game installers, or software activation tools, which are common delivery mechanisms for malware, potentially unwanted applications, and monetization campaigns.

Enable cloud-delivered protection. Verify that Microsoft Defender Antivirus cloud-delivered protection is enabled to improve detection of emerging malware and potentially unwanted applications. See: Configure cloud-delivered protection

Keep tamper protection enabled. Use tamper protection to help prevent unauthorized changes to Microsoft Defender security settings. See: Learn about tamper protection.

Enable reputation-based protection. Configure reputation-based protection to help block known malicious and untrusted applications and downloads. See: Configure reputation-based protection.

Consider Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) protections. Evaluate ASR rules, including rules that block executable files unless they meet prevalence, age, or trusted-list criteria. See: Review Attack Surface Reduction rules.

Investigation actions

Investigate execution from Inno temporary directories. Review activity from paths such as %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\, particularly when staged executables such as eld*.exe, set_*.exe, FirstFast[1].exe, or SecondRunner[1].exe are observed.

Correlate Inno callback activity. Monitor outbound requests containing d=inno together with r=offer_execution or r=offer_execution_fail, and review related process, file, and network activity across the complete installer session.

Review unexpected scheduled tasks. Investigate newly created scheduled tasks, particularly tasks running with SYSTEM privileges or recurring watchdog and updater functions. See: Audit scheduled task creation events.

Audit software inventory for unexpected installations. Review endpoints for the presence of software such as WorldProxyPool, CharityEngine, BOINC, VirtualBox, or other applications that users did not intentionally install. See: Review software inventory in Defender Vulnerability Management.

Microsoft Defender XDR detections

Microsoft Defender detects and blocks campaign-linked payloads through cloud protection, machine-learning classifications, network inspection, and behavior monitoring. Relevant observed detections include remote-thread injection, scheduled-task launch, and suspicious outbound HTTP activity.

Customers with provisioned access can also use Microsoft Security Copilot in Microsoft Defender to investigate and respond to incidents, hunt for threats, and protect their organization with relevant threat intelligence.

The vulnerability landscape continues to expand. From 1999 through September 2026, approximately 383,000 software vulnerabilities had been disclosed across platforms and technologies, yet only about 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation.

Those vulnerabilities follow clear patterns. Threat actors disproportionately target flaws that enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploit development could further shorten the window defenders have to respond.

Patching remains essential, but remediation can take weeks or months on critical systems, and some legacy or unsupported systems cannot be patched. Defenders therefore need to concentrate protection where it can have the greatest impact, considering both the likelihood of exploitation and the potential blast radius of a successful attack.

Classifying the vulnerability landscape

To make this large vulnerability population actionable, we analyzed each CVE across two dimensions: impact class and affected platform.

Impact class captures the outcome a threat actor could achieve by exploiting a vulnerability. Each CVE is assigned to the most consequential impact it directly enables. For example, when a vulnerability can bypass authentication and directly enable remote code execution (RCE), we classify it as RCE. This approach helps distinguish the underlying type of vulnerability from the security impact an attacker could achieve.

Server-side RCE: Remote code execution on a network-exposed service without user interaction.

Client-side RCE: Remote code execution that requires a user to open or run malicious content.

Local code execution: Code or command execution requiring local access or an existing foothold.

Local privilege escalation: Elevation from lower-level access to SYSTEM or root privileges.

Authentication or authorization bypass: Circumvention of authentication or access controls.

Security-control bypass: Circumvention of protections such as sandboxing, secure boot, or SmartScreen.

Information disclosure: Exposure of sensitive data or secrets.

Tampering or integrity: Unauthorized modification of data or system state.

Denial of service: Disruption of system or service availability.

Cross-site scripting (XSS): Script execution within a victim’s browser context.

Arbitrary file access: Unauthorized access to or placement of files.

Spoofing or redirect: Spoofing, redirection, or other forms of UI deception.

We also classified vulnerabilities by the platforms they affect, including Windows, Linux/Unix, mobile, network appliances, IoT/OT, virtualization hosts, and developer packages. A CVE can span multiple platforms. Developer packages are treated as a separate category because they are often cross-platform and represent a significant share of the overall vulnerability population.

Most CVEs in the analysis affect application code, including servers, web applications, browsers, productivity software, libraries, and firmware tooling, while a smaller share affects OS and system code such as kernels, drivers, and firmware.

This analysis covers CVEs published through September 2026 using Microsoft’s catalog of tracked vulnerabilities. Each CVE is counted once in the impact analysis and across each relevant platform in the platform analysis.

Figure 1 – The full published-CVE population as of September 2026, broken down by impact class and affected platform, and an OS vs. application split. Breadth dominates – many impact classes spread across many platforms, with about 77% of CVEs in application code and 23% in OS/system code.

Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild

The subset of vulnerabilities exploited in the wild is much smaller than the overall CVE population, and looks very different from it. Fewer than 1 in 200 published CVEs are ever used in a real attack, and those that do get used are overwhelmingly concentrated in the takeover classes that maximize threat actor impact and exposure.

The difference becomes clear when we look at impact. Exploitation is heavily concentrated in vulnerabilities that give attackers greater control over a system. Server-side RCE rises from 20% of published CVEs to 37% of exploited CVEs, local privilege escalation from 11% to 18%, and client-side RCE from 4% to 13%. By comparison, XSS falls from 15% to 4% and denial of service from 16% to 7%. OS vulnerabilities show a similar shift, increasing from 23% of the overall CVE population to 41% of exploited vulnerabilities.

These patterns are consistent with threat actors favoring vulnerabilities that can provide meaningful access and control. Remote code execution and privilege escalation can create footholds that support subsequent stages of an attack, while vulnerabilities that primarily cause a crash or limited script execution may offer less utility for broader compromise.

Importantly, a vulnerability’s stated classification does not always reflect what an attacker can reliably achieve in practice. For example, some vulnerabilities described as enabling RCE may ultimately result only in denial of service under real-world conditions. Understanding the demonstrated impact and exploitability of a vulnerability is therefore critical to effective prioritization.

Figure 2 – The 2,056 exploited-in-the-wild CVEs distribution, compared against the full published population: ghost lines mark each class and platform’s share of all ~380K published CVEs, and badges show the shift in percentage points. Takeover classes and OS code rise, while high-volume XSS and DoS fall.

Where defenders should focus

Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast

Patching is slow, and far slower on critical systems than others. Across platforms, servers are the critical assets and the slowest to patch. Microsoft Security Exposure Management data from 2026 shows that the median vulnerability is patched in about two weeks on Windows workstations but in more than a month on Windows Servers. It stretches to 10+ weeks on Linux Servers and for applications running on MacOS, and beyond a year on network appliances. That gap is the threat actor’s window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest.

Exploitation runs on the opposite clock: the most impactful vulnerabilities are weaponized in days, increasingly on or before disclosure. According to VulnCheck, 29% of the exploits in 2025 were launched within 1 day of CVE publication. According to CISA, the mean time from CVE publication to CISA KEV catalog fell from 89 days in 2024 to 57 days in 2025. 2026 data up to September already have that number dropping to 20 days, with a median of only 3 days since publication. Industry research suggests that advances in AI are a significant factor in the time reduction required to develop exploits, further increasing pressure on defenders to respond quickly.

Impact, exposure and where to focus

Two things determine a vulnerability’s value to a threat actor: impact and exposure. Impact is what successful exploitation provides, such as remote code execution or privilege escalation. Exposure is an asset’s position in the environment and the opportunities it creates for further compromise. An asset’s exposure is shaped by the identities, privileges, and connections available from it.

Servers often use service accounts, application identities, or cloud-managed identities with permissions beyond their operational needs. Compromising such a system can provide access to additional resources, sensitive data, administrative privileges, or trusted network paths. Together, impact and exposure determine the blast radius: a vulnerability that enables full control of a highly exposed system can enable widespread on-premises or cloud compromise.

Threat actors do not exploit at random: they go after the vulnerabilities that give the highest impact and exposure: full control of a system and the privileged identities and critical assets it has access to. As defenders, focusing on these vulnerabilities first can deliver the highest return on remediation investment.

Takeover vulnerabilities like remote code execution, authentication bypass and local privilege escalation lead here. They drive the broadest exposure and the largest blast radius, account for 78% of real-world exploited vulnerabilities, and stopping their exploitation interrupts attacks at the earliest stage, before compromise can propagate across the environment.

Next in line

A second slice deserves attention where context makes it severe: denial of service against availability-critical assets is recoverable in general, but can be mission-ending in parts of your environment where uptime is everything; disclosure of credentials or secrets can be minor as an insulated incident, but it feeds the same privileged-identity path mentioned above.

How Microsoft Security helps defenders act

Threat actors do not begin with a vulnerability list. They begin by looking for a reachable way in. Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management approaches the environment from that same outside-in perspective, continuously discovering internet-facing infrastructure, including previously unknown or unmonitored assets, shadow IT, and third-party dependencies. This gives defenders an opportunity to remove unnecessary exposure before a reachable vulnerability becomes an entry point.

Once the reachable assets are known, the next question is which weaknesses deserve immediate attention. Defenders need a way to prioritize exposure beyond CVSS alone. Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management addresses this challenge through Exposure Score and prioritized security recommendations.

Prioritization incorporates threat and exploitability signals, breach likelihood, internet exposure, and asset criticality, helping teams focus remediation on vulnerabilities that create the greatest actual exposure.

An initial foothold is only part of the risk. Attack Path Analysis connects assets and threat actor techniques into end-to-end routes from an entry point to a critical asset. Microsoft Security Exposure Management Attack Path Analysis provides a cross-workload view spanning endpoints, cloud, and hybrid environments, using vulnerability context from MDVM, endpoint data from Defender for Endpoint, and cloud asset data from Defender for Cloud. Within cloud environments, Defender CSPM Attack Path Analysis adds detailed context about internet exposure, vulnerabilities, network connections, identities, and permissions across Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud.

Together, these experiences show how an exposed workload could become a path through a privileged identity to sensitive data or another critical resource, helping defenders identify where to break the path before the initial compromise expands.

Patching remains essential, but it is not the only defensive action available. Microsoft Security helps defenders discover the doors threat actors can see, prioritize the weaknesses they are most likely to exploit, understand where a compromise could lead, and identify opportunities to break attack paths before compromise spreads to critical assets.

On October 29, 2026, Cursor reported that a tampered copy of Claude Code extension (anthropic.claude-code, versions 2.1.313 and 2.1.312) was available and served in the Cursor extension marketplace for a few hours to attempt a supply-chain attack on Cursor users. Cursor reports that it was live from about 2:27 AM to 1:35 PM Pacific Daylight Time (PDT). We have confirmed that the malicious packages found on Cursor marketplace were never published nor distributed from Microsoft Visual Studio Marketplace and from npm @antropic-ai/claude-code, which were not affected by this incident. Anthropic confirmed to Microsoft that their systems were not compromised and they did not develop the malicious package posted in Cursor marketplace. At this time, all evidence suggests that the incident is limited to Cursor marketplace.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence analyzed the injected JavaScript embedded in the malicious extension package. The injected loader runs when the extension module loads and attempts to add an attacker-controlled Secure Shell (SSH) key, enable the local SSH service, establish reverse SSH forwarding, configure persistence, and report host details. Successful remote access depends on host privileges, SSH configuration, and the attacker’s server configuration; however, the loader may still write keys and persistence artifacts even when tunnel access fails.

Organizations should identify systems that installed or automatically updated to this version from the Cursor marketplace, preserve evidence, remove confirmed malicious artifacts, review endpoint and network telemetry, and rotate credentials or revoke sessions when investigation indicates exposure. Microsoft customers can use the detections and hunting guidance in this post after the listed coverage and query validation gates are complete.

Attack chain overview

A malicious artifact associated with the Cursor Marketplace incident included a JavaScript function that executed before the extension’s expected code. When the module loads, this function can use Node.js APIs to collect host information, modify files, and execute operating-system commands. The following sections describe capabilities and attempted actions based on our analysis of the injected code.

Attack chain

The loader first collects host reconnaissance. It then attempts to install an SSH key, enable SSH, create a reverse tunnel, and configure persistence. A delayed callback subsequently attempts to send host details. The following sequence reflects code execution order; it does not prove that every step succeeded on every host.

Module loading and reconnaissance collection. The injected function executes before normal extension initialization and collects host and user information.

SSH access preparation. The loader appends an embedded public key and attempts to enable the local SSH service.

Reverse forwarding. An embedded tunnel identity authenticates an outbound connection that requests forwarding to the workstation’s SSH port.

Platform-specific persistence. Scripts and startup configuration are written to relaunch the connection.

Host reconnaissance reporting. After the access and persistence setup attempts, a delayed callback attempts to transmit the previously collected host details and selected environment-variable names.

Figure 1. Attack chain reconstructed from the injected code.

The loader uses embedded components and built-in system tools to establish persistent access without downloading another executable. It suppresses command output and silently catches errors to conceal failures and malicious activity, while the extension continues functioning normally to avoid alerting users.

Host reconnaissance collection

The loader collects the hostname, username, operating system, architecture, home directory, working directory, and global Git email. It also looks for environment-variable names containing terms such as KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASS, AWS, or GCP, keeping up to forty matches.

The callback sends matching environment-variable names, not values. This reveals potentially sensitive configuration categories but does not demonstrate theft of the secrets stored in those variables.

Collection occurs during module loading. The collected details are retained for the delayed reporting callback described after the persistence stage.

SSH authorization and tunnel identities

The loader uses two SSH identities with distinct roles. One public key authorizes access to the workstation’s user account, while a separate private key authenticates the outbound connection to the tunnel server. First, the loader checks the user’s authorized_keys file for the comment svc-telemetry. If the marker is missing, it appends an embedded Ed25519 public key. That creates an authorization entry for whoever holds the corresponding private key, subject to the local SSH server’s configuration.

Next, it decodes a separate private key for the outbound connection. The initial copy is written to a hidden temporary file named .stk_ followed by ten hexadecimal characters derived from the hostname and home directory. SSH receives that file through its -i option and connects using the remote account tunnel.

The public-key material is redacted but the format is similar to the following:

ssh-ed25519 [REDACTED PUBLIC KEY] svc-telemetry

Protocol Tunneling (T1572): reverse SSH forwarding

The tunneling SSH process is launched with the command line containing the following arguments:

-N -R '*:0:localhost:22'

It requests a listening port on the remote SSH server and forwards connections through the tunnel to port 22 on the victim’s loopback interface. The remote port value 0 asks the server to allocate a port; it does not change the local target from port 22. The -N option tells SSH not to run a command on the tunnel server.

This design starts with an outbound connection from the workstation rather than waiting for a direct inbound connection to it. The loader disables ordinary host-key checking, bypasses the normal known-hosts file, sets keepalives, and avoids interactive prompts. On Unix-like systems it prefers autossh, falling back to ssh; on Windows it uses a hidden PowerShell loop. The loops wait sixty seconds after SSH exits before retrying.

Figure 2. Terminal-style SSH command configuring an outbound reverse tunnel from a server-assigned remote port to the workstation’s local SSH service on port 22. Host-key verification is disabled, and the identity-file path is redacted.

A running SSH process does not necessarily mean the attacker gained access. Both the attacker’s server and the victim’s workstation must allow the connection, and server settings determine whether the tunnel is publicly reachable. Cursor reports that errors and administrator-permission requirements blocked SSH access on most macOS and Windows hosts. However, the malware could still attempt to plant its SSH key, establish persistence, and report host information.

Platform-specific startup persistence

The loader writes platform-specific scripts and startup configuration outside the extension directory. The following table summarizes these mechanisms and their associated artifacts. The code attempts to configure persistence, but the presence of an artifact alone does not establish that the startup mechanism ran successfully.

On Unix-like systems, the .smt script reconstructs the persistent .smtk identity when it runs, then starts its own SSH retry loop. On Windows, the loader writes the identity and batch script directly.

The startup objects use names such as SysMon and com.apple.sysmond, which resemble monitoring components. Behind these names, their configured actions invoke the generated scripts that maintain reverse SSH forwarding.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Immediate actions

Run advanced hunting queries below to identify affected systems and investigate systems where users installed or automatically updated anthropic.claude-code version 2.1.313 and 2.1.312 through the Cursor Extension Marketplace. Review extension-installation records and correlate endpoint, network, file, process, and authentication telemetry with the published indicators. Preserve the extension package, modified SSH authorization files, generated keys and scripts, and startup configuration before cleanup. Isolate devices with evidence of loader execution or backdoor installation.

Remediation actions

After evidence collection, check the affected user’s ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on macOS and Linux for the attacker-controlled key labeled svc-telemetry. On Windows, check both %USERPROFILE%\.ssh\authorized_keys and C:\ProgramData\ssh\administrators_authorized_keys, where present. Confirm the key against the fingerprint in Indicators of Compromise before removing the exact unauthorized entry. Preserve unrelated SSH keys and legitimate remote-development configuration. A missing marker alone should not replace review of the installation, process, network, and persistence evidence.

Remove the trojanized extension and confirmed malicious persistence after evidence collection. Inspect each startup object’s configured action before removal; names alone are not sufficient to distinguish malicious objects from legitimate monitoring software.

macOS: Unload and remove the malicious user LaunchAgent at ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist and remove its associated ~/.config/.smt script and ~/.config/.smtk identity.

Linux: Remove the malicious user-crontab @reboot entry referencing ~/.config/.smt, preserving unrelated entries, and remove the associated script and ~/.config/.smtk identity.

Windows: Remove the malicious SysMon scheduled task, the Startup-folder sysmon.cmd fallback, and associated %USERPROFILE%\.config\smt.cmd and %USERPROFILE%\.config\smtk files.

All applicable platforms: Stop confirmed malicious SSH and retry processes and remove their temporary .stk_ identity files after collection.

Cursor published platform-specific checks and remediation scripts in its security notice. Review the scripts and execution requirements before use, then verify that no listed artifacts remain. Cleanup does not replace investigation of device activity during the exposure window.

Removing or updating the extension does not remove artifacts written outside its installation directory. Remove confirmed unauthorized SSH keys, tunnel identities, scripts, and startup entries separately. Cursor’s reported server takedown does not remove artifacts already present on a device.

Follow-up Investigation and recovery

Review telemetry after the extension loaded for SSH key acceptance, tunnel processes, local SSH sessions, command execution, and file activity. Rotate credentials and revoke sessions from a known-clean device when telemetry indicates credential access or when device trust cannot be restored. Rebuild the device when required by the investigation and verify that the tunnel and startup artifacts do not return after login or restart.

To reduce the risk of malicious extensions and extension-based supply chain attacks, organizations using Cursor should apply the relevant controls in Cursor’s security-hardening guidance, including restricting extensions to approved publishers and configuring an extension installation cooldown to delay installation of newly published versions. These measures can help limit exposure to malicious releases.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence investigated two human-operated intrusions in which threat actors used Microsoft Teams messages and calls to impersonate IT or help desk personnel and socially engineer users into granting interactive remote access, primarily through Quick Assist. Once connected, the threat actors staged portable Python, Bun, or Java runtimes, performed host and network discovery, and assessed Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) for certificate-based authentication paths.

Although the incidents began with the same social-engineering and remote-access pattern, they diverged at the certificate layer. In Case 1, the threat actor abused an Enterprise CA Security Configuration 1 (ESC1) -vulnerable certificate template to obtain authentication certificates for privileged accounts and performed DCSync. In Case 2, the threat actor used PetitPotam, a technique that causes a Windows server to authenticate to an attacker-controlled system. The attacker relayed the domain controller’s New Technology (NT) LAN Manager (NTLM) authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment (ESC8), obtained a certificate for the domain-controller account, and used it for certificate-based Kerberos authentication (PKINIT – Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication).

This intrusion pattern is high impact because a user-approved remote session can become certificate-backed access to privileged identities and domain infrastructure. In Case 1, Microsoft Defender attack disruption restricted covered identities and blocked substantial follow-on activity, but a privileged identity excluded from automated containment remained usable and later supported data exfiltration. In Case 2, Defender generated ESC8-related alerts, after which the customer isolated the associated workstation and no further progression was observed. The activity did not exploit a vulnerability in Microsoft Teams; instead, it relied on social engineering and insecure or overly permissive AD CS configurations.

In this blog, we analyze the shared attack chain, the ESC1 and ESC8 certificate-abuse paths, and the different response outcomes. We also provide investigation methods, mitigation recommendations, Microsoft Defender detection guidance, and advanced hunting queries to help defenders identify and interrupt this access path. The activity described here is not attributed to a specific threat actor.

Activity overview

Risk to enterprise environments

AD CS can turn a certificate request into a durable authentication path. An attacker who obtains an authentication certificate for a privileged user or machine account can use that certificate independently of the initially compromised password. Resetting the user’s password or reimaging the first workstation does not revoke an issued certificate or invalidate Kerberos tickets that have already been issued.

Two AD CS abuse techniques are central to these incidents:

ESC1 – certificate template abuse: A low-privileged requester abuses a misconfigured authentication-capable template that permits requester-supplied identity information and broad enrollment, allowing the requester to obtain a certificate for a privileged account.

ESC8 – NTLM relay to Web Enrollment: An attacker relays a user or machine account’s NTLM authentication to an AD CS web enrollment endpoint that lacks relay protections, then requests a certificate as the relayed identity.

Attackers can use Microsoft Teams to impersonate IT support personnel and persuade users to approve a remote session, gaining hands-on-keyboard access without a conventional malware attachment.

Portable or renamed runtimes such as Python, Bun, and Java can execute attacker-controlled scripts from user-writable locations while retaining legitimate file metadata.

Automated disruption is most effective when every compromised identity and device remains eligible for containment; exclusions can preserve the attacker’s path.

Attack chain overview

Both incidents followed the same initial sequence: help desk impersonation through Teams, a user-approved Quick Assist or other remote-support session, archive transfer and extraction, portable runtime execution, and host and AD CS discovery. The certificate technique and response outcome then split into two distinct branches.

Figure 1. Both incidents followed a shared entry and execution pattern before diverging into two AD CS abuse paths. Case 1 used an ESC1-vulnerable certificate template to obtain certificates for privileged identities. Case 2 used PetitPotam to coerce domain-controller authentication and relay it to AD CS Web Enrollment through ESC8. The response outcomes differed based on containment coverage and removal of the active execution point.

Shared initial access and execution pattern

Teams helpdesk impersonation and remote access

Both incidents began with Teams phishing messages and calls that impersonated support personnel. The social engineering persuaded a user to establish an attacker-controlled remote session, primarily by guiding the user to open Quick Assist and provide the connection code. This gave the attacker hands-on-keyboard access to the workstation. Across the broader activity, organization-themed onmicrosoft.com tenant names and support-oriented display names were used to make the external contact appear familiar.

Figure 2. Example Teams call displaying External and Scam suspected indicators. These labels are important user-facing signals during support impersonation attempts.

The remote session was the decisive transition in the attack. Immediately after the user granted control through Quick Assist, the attacker used the session to place an archive in the victim’s Downloads folder. Commands launched during the session created a KB-prefixed staging directory under the user’s profile, extracted the archive into that directory, and started the included payload with a portable Python, JavaScript, or Java runtime. The payload then performed host and network discovery and began assessing AD CS.

Portable runtime staging and execution variants

The runtime and packaging varied between deployments, but the execution pattern remained consistent: an archive was placed on the device during the remote session, extracted into a newly created user-profile directory, and used to launch attacker-controlled code. In one JavaScript variant, a renamed executable retained version metadata identifying it as the Bun runtime and launched the staged loader. A separate variant used a staged Java runtime to launch a Java source file.

Figure 3. Sanitized Bun staging command. The update-themed path, renamed runtime, script operand, and remote-session context form the useful investigation pattern.

File names alone are weak indicators. The actionable pattern is a portable runtime launched from a newly created, user-writable staging directory after an unauthorized remote session, followed by script execution, discovery commands, or connections to identity infrastructure.

Figure 4. Sanitized Java staging variant. The campaign could substitute runtime and packaging choices while keeping the broader access pattern.

The Java variant confirms that runtime choice can change between deployments. The AD CS behavior in each incident should be validated through the initiating process, account, device, and certificate records rather than assumed from the presence of Bun or Java alone.

Host discovery and AD CS assessment

The staged components queried Windows version information, network configuration, and running processes. These commands are common in administration, but they become high-value signals when it is launched by a renamed runtime from an uncommon location and follow an unexpected remote-support session.

Figure 5. Host-discovery commands from the first draft. Their value comes from the initiating staged runtime, user-writable path, and preceding unauthorized remote session.

The compromised workstation also connected to domain infrastructure using LDAPS and SMB.

From this shared workstation foothold, the incidents followed different certificate-abuse paths. In Case 1, the attacker exploited an ESC1-vulnerable certificate template. In Case 2, the attacker used PetitPotam to coerce domain-controller authentication and relay it to AD CS Web Enrollment through ESC8.

Case 1: ESC1 abuse and the cost of an identity exclusion

ESC1 certificate requests expand privilege

The first Teams-phishing wave targeted three user accounts and compromised one workstation. From the shared foothold described above, the attacker examined AD CS for a privilege-escalation path.

Figure 6. Case 1: Help desk impersonation led to ESC1 certificate abuse. Attack disruption restricted most compromised identities, but an excluded privileged account remained usable and later supported data exfiltration.

The attacker found a certificate template vulnerable to ESC1. ESC1 describes a template configuration in which a requester can supply identity information in the certificate request and obtain a certificate that supports authentication. When broad enrollment rights and weak issuance controls are combined with that setting, a low-privileged account can request a certificate representing a privileged identity.

In the first wave, the attacker obtained certificates for three highly privileged accounts. Microsoft Defender attack disruption targeted the initially compromised user and those three certificate-compromised identities. Remote logons and Server Message Block (SMB) access were restricted and active sessions were disconnected. One privileged account was excluded from automated response, so containment did not apply to that identity.

Renewed phishing and ESC1 privilege expansion

About 90 minutes after the first disrupted session, the attacker launched a larger Teams-phishing wave targeting 16 users and compromised another workstation. The attacker again abused the ESC1-vulnerable template, this time obtaining certificates for eight additional privileged accounts.

Attack disruption targeted the newly compromised user and the eight certificate-compromised identities. More than 1,000 subsequent SMB file-access attempts and additional logon attempts were blocked, limiting the attacker’s ability to reuse those accounts for lateral movement.

DCSync, the excluded account, and data theft

Within seconds of obtaining one privileged certificate, the attacker authenticated to a domain controller and performed DCSync while containment was taking effect. Attack disruption limited additional replication and follow-on use, but the operation had already begun.

The privileged account excluded during the first disruption remained available. The attacker continued to use it for network and remote-interactive logons, reached a file server, and launched a renamed copy of Rclone using the filename SearchApp.exe. The command recursively copied data from a file-server share to an external Secure File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) destination, used 20 concurrent transfers, selected files up to three years old, and excluded several executable, database, virtual-disk, media, temporary, and log file types.

Figure 7. Sanitized Rclone command used to copy data from a file-server share to an external SFTP destination.

The incident demonstrates that partial identity containment can reduce attack activity while still leaving a viable privileged route.

Case 2: PetitPotam and ESC8 turn a workstation into a domain-controller identity

PetitPotam coerces domain-controller authentication

The ESC1 path used in the first case was not available in this environment. Instead, the attacker used PetitPotam to send requests over the Encrypting File System Remote Protocol (EFSRPC), causing the domain controller to authenticate to an attacker-controlled system using its machine account. The attacker then relayed that NTLM authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment without knowing the domain controller’s password.

Figure 8. Case 2: Help desk impersonation led to PetitPotam authentication coercion, ESC8 relay to AD CS, certificate-based Kerberos authentication, and customer-led device isolation.

NTLM relay reaches AD CS Web Enrollment

The attacker relayed the domain controller’s NTLM authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment. This technique is known as ESC8. It targets an enrollment web endpoint that accepts NTLM without sufficient relay protection, allowing the attacker to submit a certificate request as the relayed account.

The AD CS server authenticated the domain-controller machine account even though the connection originated from another device. That identity-to-source mismatch is a strong investigation pivot: correlate the machine account, source device, Web Enrollment request, Certification Authority (CA) issuance record, and subsequent Kerberos activity.

After authenticating to Web Enrollment as the domain controller, the attacker requested and retrieved a certificate using the Domain Controller template. The important service paths are the certificate submission and retrieval endpoints under /certsrv; isolated URL access is not malicious by itself and must be correlated with the authenticated identity, source device, process, and CA request.

Figure 9. Sanitized view of AD CS Web Enrollment activity involving certificate submission and retrieval through /certsrv, used during ESC8 certificate issuance for a relayed domain-controller identity.

Certificate-based Kerberos authentication

The attacker used the newly issued domain-controller certificate for Kerberos PKINIT and obtained a ticket-granting ticket (TGT) for the domain controller. This step converted a relayed NTLM authentication into a certificate-backed Kerberos identity.

PKINIT success is the response threshold: responders should investigate the requesting device, authenticated account, issued certificate, active Kerberos sessions, and any service-ticket use. Certificate revocation and Kerberos ticket review are separate containment actions.

Customer-led device isolation and observed outcome

Microsoft Defender generated ESC8-related alerts, after which the customer isolated the workstation associated with the certificate-enrollment and Kerberos activity. The documented containment action in this case was customer-led device isolation. No further attack progression was observed following isolation.

Why the response outcomes differed

In Case 1, an exclusion left a compromised privileged account available to the attacker despite disruption of other identities. In Case 2, customer-led device isolation followed Defender alerts, and no further attack progression was observed.

Actionable investigation methods

The most useful artifacts are not individual commands or ports in isolation. Investigators should reconstruct the chain across collaboration, endpoint, identity, and certificate systems.

Teams and remote access: identify the external tenant, user interaction, call or chat timing, remote-session start, approved remote monitoring and management (RMM) process, and child processes created during the session.

Runtime staging: inspect newly created KB-prefixed or application-like folders, archive extraction, runtime metadata, script operands, parent-child relationships, and subsequent network activity.

Directory interaction: use network data to identify LDAPS and SMB connections, then use endpoint and directory logs to determine what the initiating process did. TLS intentionally hides LDAP query content from passive network inspection.

ESC1: review certificate request and issuance events, requester identity, subject and Subject Alternative Names (SAN) values, template name, enrollment permissions, and the first authentication performed with the issued certificate.

PetitPotam and ESC8: correlate EFSRPC activity, outbound authentication by the domain controller, the device that relayed the authentication, Web Enrollment access, CA request and issuance records, and PKINIT from the originating workstation.

Disruption and containment: enumerate every compromised identity and device, review exclusions before and during response, revoke unauthorized certificates, and assess active Kerberos tickets separately

Reduce support impersonation and unauthorized remote access

Require users to verify unsolicited support requests through a known internal channel before joining a call, sharing a screen, or starting a remote-control session.

Encourage users to pay attention to warnings in incoming messages and calls when impersonation is detected.

Review Teams external-access and federation policies. Limit external domains to business requirements and investigate newly observed organization-themed or helpdesk-themed tenants in context.

Restrict remote-support software to approved products, operators, and workflows. Alert when approved RMM tools extract archives, create interpreters, or launch scripts from user-writable paths.

Constrain runtime-based execution

Use App Control for Business or equivalent application control to restrict unapproved portable runtimes and script execution from user-writable locations.

Evaluate file identity through signer, original filename, product metadata, path, parent process, and behavior. A renamed executable can retain legitimate version information.

Test relevant attack surface reduction rules and endpoint protection policies. Do not assume controls for Windows script hosts automatically cover JavaScript executed through Bun or source files launched through Java.

Harden AD CS against ESC1 and ESC8

Follow Microsoft’s secure configuration guidance for mitigating NTLM relay against AD CS: https://support.microsoft.com/help/5005413

Review authentication-capable templates for requester-supplied subject information, broad enrollment permissions, weak issuance requirements, and excessive certificate purpose. Remove unnecessary enrollment rights and require approval where appropriate.

Inventory AD CS Web Enrollment and Certificate Enrollment Web Service endpoints. Remove endpoints that are not required.

Require HTTPS and enforce Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on enrollment web endpoints. HTTPS protects confidentiality; EPA provides the channel binding needed to resist NTLM relay.

Disable NTLM on enrollment services where operationally feasible and validate Kerberos-only authentication before broad enforcement.

Use Defender for Identity AD CS security posture assessments to identify ESC1-related template exposure and insecure enrollment Internet Information Services (IIS) endpoints associated with ESC8: https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-for-identity/security-posture-assessments/certificates

Enable certificate auditing and prepare certificate-aware response

Enable the Certification Services advanced audit subcategory for success and failure, and configure the Certification Authority audit filter to record request and issuance activity.

Preserve CA security events, CA database records, IIS or Web Enrollment logs, endpoint process lineage, identity alerts, and Teams interaction records.

If an unauthorized certificate was issued, identify its serial number and thumbprint, revoke it, publish updated revocation information, and confirm that relying systems can obtain the update.

Review certificate-based Kerberos activity and active tickets. Revoking a certificate does not retroactively invalidate TGTs or service tickets that were already issued.

Treat containment exclusions as incident decisions. If an account or device cannot be automatically contained, assign a compensating manual action and verify completion.

In this article

Stages of AI adoption by North Korean threat actors

AI use across North Korean threat operations

AI-assisted targeting and reconnaissance

AI-assisted social engineering and identity deception

AI-assisted software and tooling development

AI-assisted operational scaling and analysis

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft Defender detections

As Microsoft Threat Intelligence continues to track how threat actors operationalize AI to increase the speed, efficiency, and complexity of attacks, we’ve identified North Korean threat actors expanding their use of AI with varying levels of adoption. Threat actors use AI as a force multiplier across their operations, particularly to accelerate and scale established workflows.

Recent activities illustrate this AI-enabled acceleration and scaling: Jade Sleet launched campaigns through three front companies in a single week, Onyx Sleet generated dozens of tailored lures in minutes, Coral Sleet rapidly built a new capability to trojanize private source code repositories, and Diamond Sleet used AI to enhance tailored targeting workflows, including persona development and front company creation. Further, Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet are leveraging the open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to conduct operations, further indicating North Korea’s willingness to quickly adopt new AI technologies for their operations.

The Democratic People’s Republic of Korea operates under extensive international sanctions and uses cyber operations and other illicit mechanisms to evade these restrictions and advance state objectives. Within this operating environment, North Korean threat actors have adopted new technologies that help sustain or advance existing operations. AI adoption by North Korean threat actors therefore largely supports existing goals and targeting priorities rather than representing a shift in actor motivations. North Korean threat actors conduct cyber operations primarily to generate revenue for the regime, collect strategic intelligence, and, in some cases, pursue politically motivated disruptive or destructive objectives. Across these objectives, North Korean threat actor tradecraft remains grounded in social engineering, malware delivery, and the abuse of legitimate tools. These operations commonly target cryptocurrency and financial organizations, information technology companies and software supply chains, government entities, and education-related organizations. Despite threat actors’ adoption of AI, Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that AI-enabled operations remain human-directed and have not become fully autonomous.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses the overall adoption of AI across North Korean threat actors as high, with threat actors such as Jade Sleet, Coral Sleet, and Jasper Sleet demonstrating an established use of AI across all operational workflows, alongside increasing adoption across the broader North Korean threat actor set. This blog breaks down how North Korean threat actors are utilizing AI across their operations, reflecting a broader trend of threat actors incorporating AI into their attack chains. We also provide mitigation guidance and Microsoft Defender detections to help organizations defend against these threats.

Stages of AI adoption by North Korean threat actors

North Korean threat actors are increasingly integrating generative and agentic AI platforms into their operations, but the rate and maturity of adoption vary. Based on identified AI use, Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses high-impact North Korean threat actors across four stages of adoption: emerging, expanding, accelerating, and operationalized. Across these actors, AI use spans research, content generation, development, malware and tooling, infrastructure, and broader operational activities.

Mapping high-impact North Korean threat actors by stages of AI adoption

Operationalized: Threat actors at this stage have embedded AI into routine operational workflows, using it as an established part of their existing processes. Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that the North Korean threat actors Jade Sleet, Coral Sleet, and Jasper Sleet have operationalized AI across their entire operations, which frequently encompass identity-based attacks built on deceptive social engineering. These attacks can be accelerated with AI capabilities that tailor lures or personas to the intended audience.

Accelerating: Threat actors at this stage demonstrate rapid adoption of AI across multiple operational functions. Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that Diamond Sleet, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, and Sapphire Sleet are at the accelerating stage of AI adoption.

Expanding: Threat actors at this stage are expanding their use of AI across selected operational activities, but adoption is not yet embedded across broader workflows. Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that Emerald Sleet is at the expanding stage of AI adoption. While evidence suggests Emerald Sleet has incorporated AI into some workflows, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has not identified the same level of adoption and impact as other North Korean threat actors.

Emerging: Threat actors at this stage demonstrate limited or experimental use of AI. At this time, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has not assessed any North Korean threat actors as operating at the emerging stage.

AI use across North Korean threat operations

Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified North Korean threat actors using AI platforms to support a range of operational activities, from reconnaissance to developing social engineering content, maintaining fraudulent identities, supporting tool development, and scaling repetitive operational tasks. Current evidence indicates that these actors primarily use AI to enhance existing tradecraft and operator productivity rather than to enable autonomous operations. Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified North Korean threat actors leveraging the following AI-enabled tactics as part of their threat operations.

AI-assisted targeting and reconnaissance

Based on industry reporting and changes in targeting activity in 2026, North Korean threat actors are scaling reconnaissance capabilities by using generative AI platforms, including gathering information on target organizations prior to launching social engineering operations. Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified that these actors:

Research organizations and employees, then use information from this research to craft highly bespoke and convincing lures, target-specific infrastructure, and job applications

Research wallets, exchanges, and decentralized finance (DeFi) and blockchain workflows, accelerating the development of domain knowledge needed to support targeted operations

Explore vulnerabilities, APIs, security products, and cloud services, leading to a demonstrated change in the speed and sophistication of threat activity against specific technologies

Research software development roles, job requirements, and technology organizations to support job searching, resume development, and persona alignment, resulting in rapid tailored persona or lure creation, application to newly posted job roles, or spear-phishing operations

For example, between June 8 and June 12, 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified Jade Sleet conducting job-themed targeting against individuals across various organizations, including those involved in cybersecurity, AI, blockchain, and talent recruitment companies. The actor leveraged tailored domains, social media profiles, and industry-specific knowledge to pose as recruiters for a spoofed AI-powered blockchain intelligence company, using software engineer-themed opportunities to initiate contact and schedule interviews with individuals who engaged with the outreach. Within this short time frame, Jade Sleet conducted similar job-themed targeting using two additional front companies, supported by comparable infrastructure and relevant domain knowledge. Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that the pace and breadth of this activity demonstrate how Jade Sleet is using generative AI to accelerate operational workflows, including rapidly developing target- and industry-specific knowledge, tailoring reconnaissance and targeting, and scaling outreach to target individuals.

Jasper Sleet also continues to leverage generative AI platforms to build fake digital personas. The actor’s suspected use of generative and agentic AI-assisted resume workflows demonstrates an improvement in the speed, scale, and relevance of persona preparation over the past year. Identified application activity indicates that the actor has invested in repeatable tooling to support employment-themed operations, ultimately helping the actor scale application activity and interact more credibly with the hiring processes of impacted organizations.

Since August 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed Diamond Sleet returning to targeting the oil and gas sector for the first time since 2023, expanding their focus on communications and internet policy-related organizations, and continuing to target defense-related organizations. Further, Diamond Sleet has created fake communications technology companies, complete with supporting websites and tailored personas, to target telecommunications companies under the guise of legitimate business partnerships. These shifts have occurred alongside Diamond Sleet’s increased use of generative AI platforms to support reconnaissance and technical development, suggesting that AI could be improving the efficiency of existing operational workflows.

AI-assisted social engineering and identity deception

Several North Korean threat actors leverage job-themed social engineering techniques to gain access to target environments. For example, Sapphire Sleet, Jade Sleet, and Coral Sleet use employment- and interview-themed social engineering to target users and organizations, while Jasper Sleet uses fraudulent identities to obtain legitimate remote employment. These actors leverage AI to improve the process of creating convincing lures, aid in the development of fake personas, and evade detection when interacting with targets. Specifically, these actors use AI to:

Produce tailored phishing, recruiter, and investment lures

Create job-themed payload-delivery content and malicious repository lures

Translate content and adjust tone to support foreign-language impersonation and more natural communications

Build resumes, biographies, and realistic interview responses

Support coding assessments, job-related tasks, and the management of multiple worker personas

Enhance profile images and other identity artifacts

Alter profile images, video, voice, and backgrounds

Sustain recruiter, developer, investor, and other social identities across interactions and platforms

Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified over 100 PDF lure files attributed to Onyx Sleet that were created in August and September 2026 with target-specific details. Metadata indicated that the actor created dozens of files at a time in rapid succession within minutes, highly likely to be the output of an AI platform. This automation supports the actor’s high-volume phishing campaigns against South Korean users and could make disruption and detection efforts more difficult given the rapid regeneration or modification of additional lures.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence has also identified possible synthetic media generation, focused on AI-created voice and video, by Emerald Sleet. While we have not been able to determine the full operational impact of such tooling, it is highly likely that synthetic media creation is valued by multiple North Korean threat actors, as it significantly enhances existing social engineering capabilities.

AI-assisted software and tooling development

Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified evidence indicating that North Korean threat actors are leveraging AI-enabled software and tools to assist in malware development. These tools include AI-assisted development platforms, such as Cursor, which have likely enabled Jade Sleet, Coral Sleet, Pearl Sleet, and Sapphire Sleet to:

Generate, convert, debug, and refactor code

Assist with scripts, commands, persistence mechanisms, and obfuscation

Troubleshoot errors and help operators diagnose tool behavior

Support the adaptation or reimplementation of functionality across languages, libraries, and environments

Additionally, AI-enabled development cycles further allow threat actors to circumvent detection and blocking efforts, as AI platforms streamline retooling, helping enable threat actors to rapidly pivot in reaction to defensive measures.

For example, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified evidence indicating that Sapphire Sleet, who has conducted several supply chain attacks, likely incorporated AI during the August 2026 Rust software compromise. The activity spanned from initial stages targeting Rust developers to development and deployment of malware. Notably, Sapphire Sleet’s malware in this campaign was a marked improvement compared with other attributed campaigns, as the malware used dynamic .NET compilation during post-exploitation, most likely for defense evasion.

And, since April 2026, Coral Sleet has operationalized a workflow to trojanize private GitHub repositories, integrating them into their existing malware chain. This new capability, its breadth and scale, and its rapid implementation were highly likely engineered using an AI-enabled development platform.

AI-assisted operational scaling and analysis

North Korean threat actors are leveraging AI platforms to scale and manage diverse operations. For example, Jasper Sleet’s AI tooling helps maintain consistent communication and performance across multiple fraudulent worker personas. We have also seen evidence of AI use for automating repetitive tasks, summarizing collected information from victim organizations, and accelerating post-compromise decision making while human operators likely continue to direct intent and objectives. This operational adoption extends to emerging agentic AI technologies. Since late October 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet leveraging open-source agentic AI penetration testing ARTEX in operations, highlighting how North Korean threat actors are adopting new AI technologies as they become available.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Threat actor misuse of AI accelerates risk across enterprise environments by amplifying existing threats such as phishing, malware threats, and insider activity. To help organizations stay ahead of AI-enabled threat activity, Microsoft has introduced the Security Dashboard for AI. The dashboard provides users with a unified view of AI security posture by aggregating security, identity, and data risk across Microsoft Defender, Microsoft Entra, and Microsoft Purview. This allows organizations to understand what AI assets exist in their environment, recognize emerging risk patterns, and prioritize governance and security across AI agents, applications, and platforms. To learn more about the Microsoft Security Dashboard for AI see: Assess your organization’s AI risk with Microsoft Security Dashboard for AI.

Additionally, Microsoft Agent 365 serves as a control plane for AI agents in enterprise environments, allowing users to manage, govern, and secure AI agents and workflows while monitoring emerging risks of agentic AI use. Agent 365 supports a growing ecosystem of agents, including Microsoft agents, broader ecosystems of agents such as Adobe and Databricks, and open-source agents published on GitHub.

As the AI-enabled operations conducted by North Korean threat actors vary across tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs), the following guidance can help organizations harden their networks against multiple classes of threats.

Vulnerability and exposure management

Use Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management to identify, assess, remediate, and track vulnerabilities across critical assets. Use the exposure score to reduce your vulnerability exposure and the Microsoft Secure Score to identify and remediate security misconfigurations in your environment.

Use a perimeter scanning tool like Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management to understand your organization’s digital footprint and potential attack surface. Targeting web-facing vulnerabilities continues to be one of the most effective attack methods for initial access.

Ensure any web-facing systems are isolated from the public internet with a secure network boundary and access them with a virtual private network (VPN). If certain servers must be accessible on the public internet, position them behind a web application firewall (WAF), reverse proxy, or perimeter network (also known as a DMZ), which can reduce the risk of vulnerability exploitation in some cases.

Consider automating patching where possible. Windows Update client policies offer automated patching, which can greatly reduce the amount of time IT admins must spend identifying, configuring, and deploying updates.

To help manage infrastructure distributed across cloud, on-premises, and hybrid networks, use a centralized patching solution like Azure Update Manager.

Protecting against social engineering and phishing

Educate users about protecting personal and business information on social media, filtering unsolicited communication, identifying lures in spear-phishing emails and watering holes, and reporting reconnaissance attempts and other suspicious activity.

Educate users about preventing malware infections, such as ignoring or deleting unsolicited and unexpected emails or attachments sent through instant messaging applications or social networks.

Review the recommended settings for Exchange Online Protection and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to ensure your organization has established essential defenses and knows how to monitor and respond to threat activity.

Invest in user awareness training and phishing simulations. Attack simulation training in Microsoft Defender for Office 365, which also includes simulating phishing messages in Microsoft Teams, is one approach to running realistic attack scenarios in your organization.

Enable Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) in Defender for Office 365 to quarantine sent mail in response to newly acquired threat intelligence and retroactively neutralize malicious phishing, spam, or malware messages that have already been delivered to mailboxes.

Responders could also manually check for and purge unwanted emails containing URLs and/or Subject fields that are similar, but not identical, to those of known bad messages.

Investigate malicious email that was delivered in Microsoft 365 and use Threat Explorer to find and delete phishing emails.

Turn on Safe Links and Safe Attachments in Microsoft Defender for Office 365.

Only allow device code flow where necessary. Microsoft recommends blocking device code flow wherever possible. Where necessary, configure Microsoft Entra ID’s device code flow in your Conditional Access policies.

Vetting potential employees

Exercise greater scrutiny for employees of staffing companies, since this is the easiest avenue for North Korean workers to infiltrate target companies.

Check to make sure a potential employee’s social media/professional accounts are not highly similar to the accounts of other individuals. In addition, check that a contact phone number listed on a potential employee’s account is unique and not also used by other accounts.

Scrutinize resumes and background checks for consistency of names, addresses, and dates. Consider contacting references by phone or video-teleconference rather than email only.

Search whether a potential employee is employed at multiple companies using the same persona.

Ensure the potential employee is seen on camera during multiple video telecommunication sessions. If the potential employee reports video and/or microphone issues that prohibit participation, this should be considered a red flag.

Confirm the potential employee has a digital footprint. This includes a real phone number (not VOIP), a residential address, and social media accounts.

Defending against malware

Turn on cloud-delivered protection in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.

Ensure Microsoft Defender Antivirus definitions are up to date and real-time protection is turned on.

Run endpoint detection and response (EDR) in block mode so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.

Configure investigation and remediation in full automated mode to let Microsoft Defender for Endpoint take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.

Configure automatic attack disruption in Microsoft Defender XDR. Automatic attack disruption is designed to contain attacks in progress, limit the impact on an organization’s assets, and provide more time for security teams to remediate the attack fully.

Title: The CISO’s evolving role: Protecting and defending in the agentic era
Context: And we have to rethink how we defend that enterprise as attackers use AI to move faster and operate at greater scale
Full Text:
October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month, and it’s a good time to think about how much the world has changed for chief information security officers (CISOs) in the last 12 months.

A year ago, we thought we were already in the thick of AI and starting to understand it. Since then, agents have spread across the enterprise faster than most organizations anticipated. According to our Work Trend Index Annual Report, the number of active agents in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem grew 15-fold year over year and 18-fold in large enterprises. Employees are building and deploying AI systems that can access company data, interact with applications, and take actions on their behalf. These systems are built with good intentions, but even well-intentioned agents can introduce risk when access and behavior are not appropriately governed.

At the same time, more people inside our companies are building with AI. Many of them haven’t written code in years, if ever, and they aren’t necessarily thinking about security the way a security team would. That isn’t a criticism. It’s how quickly the technology has expanded who can build and what they can accomplish.

For CISOs, this creates two fundamental shifts. We have to protect an enterprise that increasingly operates through AI and agents. And we have to rethink how we defend that enterprise as attackers use AI to move faster and operate at greater scale. When I talk with CISOs, these are the two challenges I keep coming back to. We need to enable innovation without introducing unmanaged risk, and we need to modernize defense without losing the security fundamentals that still matter.

Get the 2026 Work Trend Index report

For builders: Build securely in the agentic era

Cybersecurity awareness has always been about people. This year, it has to include the people building agents. If you’re a developer, a builder, or someone who has just realized that AI can help you design and build things, this part is for you.

Give your agents their own identities. Where supported and appropriate, assign agents governed identities rather than personal or shared credentials. When something goes wrong, you need to know which agent did it and be able to shut it off.

Protect the data your agents touch. If an agent can reach information, assume it will use it. Make sure the right data protections are in place before you connect it. And remember that the agent will not think like you. It doesn’t share your judgment or your sense of what is appropriate. If you give it access to information or systems, it will act on that access, and that can quickly become a problem.

Your CISO wants you to build. They also need to know what’s being built, so they can help you do it safely. The best thing you can do for your security leader is to have the identity and data conversation early, before you build, not after.

For CISOs: Protect the enterprise as agent adoption grows

Your first job is to put guardrails in place so people can innovate carefully, without slowing them down. Good guardrails help teams move faster because they know where the lines are.

Start with observability, and make it deep. You need to know which agents exist, who owns them, what they can reach, and what they’re doing. You can’t protect what you can’t see. Deep observability also means knowing when an agent’s behavior changes, so your team can step in before a small issue becomes a big one.

Then hold people’s feet to the fire on identity and data. These are the two areas where I wouldn’t give any ground. Every agent needs a governed identity with only the access it needs, and the data it can reach needs to be classified and protected. When those two are in place, most other decisions get easier. Here’s how we’re approaching agent governance.

For CISOs: Defending differently

Your second job is to defend differently than you have historically done.

Attackers are using AI to move faster, and our latest Microsoft Digital Defense Report shows how much that is compressing the time defenders have to respond. But defending differently isn’t simply about adopting faster tools. It’s about changing how security teams turn information into action. The more integrated your environment is, the faster you’ll be able to see an attack and respond to it. An attack rarely shows up in just one place. Signals across identity, endpoints, applications, and cloud environments need to come together with threat intelligence and organizational context so defenders can understand what’s happening and respond before an incident escalates. When your tools work together, your team sees the full picture instead of pieces of it. It also requires a security approach built to continuously assess risk, make decisions, and act at the speed threats are developing.

You also need the right threat intelligence and the right partner. Threat intelligence helps organizations understand how threats are changing, which ones matter to their environment, and where to focus their defenses. Working with partners that have visibility across industries and organizations can provide broader context than an individual organization may have on its own. And you’re not going to operate at this speed without agents helping you. The same capabilities that make attacks faster can make defense faster, with agents working alongside your analysts to investigate and respond. That’s why we’re bringing integrated security operations and agentic defense together.

Two jobs, one goal

The pace of change over the last year has been significant, and it is likely to continue. None of this means slowing down. The CISOs I talk with want their companies to innovate. They need to protect the enterprise as it uses AI and the increasing speed of AI-enabled threats.

Prepare for an agent-driven workplace

Explore Work Trend Index insights on the changing role of agents at work and the trends shaping how organizations operate.

Explore the Work Trend Index

If you’re building with AI, bring your security team in early and have the identity and data conversation. If you’re a CISO, focus on those two jobs and make sure you have the right partners for both.

Title: Inside the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: Credential theft through Python startup hooks
Context: Attack overview LiteLLM is commonly deployed as a gateway between applications and model providers
